description: Hi, we're Astro united, a group of students and tech enthusiast with a strong background in robotics, hardware development, and artificial intelligence. our technical skills range from building sensor-driven hardware (such as an Arduino-based firefighting robot and a smart air quality monitor for Lalitpur) to working with cloud infrastructure and advanced AI tools like NVIDIA NIM, AWS, and frontier LLM models.
summary:
Astro-Mars is an interactive web map of Jezero crater on Mars, bringing together real data from multiple credible sources and lining it all up on one shared map that anyone can explore in a browser.

Users can click any spot to see its features. They can plan routes that avoid dangerous slopes and rough terrain, save waypoints, and browse Perseverance's latest photos. A Survival Hub imagines how astronauts could use the map in an emergency

Mars data is free but scattered, hard to read and usually needs specialist software. Jezero Explorer removes that barrier and turns raw scientific data into something students, teachers and space fans can explore and ask questions about.

It aims to make Mars feel like a real place to navigate and not some distant alien planet
details:
Astro-Mars is an interactive map featuring the area and terrain of the Jezero crater on Mars

Why Jezero?

  • The same reason NASA sent Perseverance there : the intriguing and thought-provoking delta deposits in the region
  • We wanted to build something connected to an active mission.
  • It's one of the best-mapped places on Mars with interesting terrain
  • We believed it was better to cover one specific area properly than to map the entire Mars in a sloppy manner

What does Astro-Mars do?

  • Presents multiple credible datasets in the form of toggleable layers
  • Clicking on any point on the map shows intricate detail about the location
  • Plans a route for you (Using A* algorithm to find a path that avoids steep slopes and rough ground)
  • Allows you to save waypoints
  • Lets you browse Perseverance's raw images straight from NASA's public API feed
  • Features the Survival Hub, a proof-of-concept, consisting of a set of emergency scenarios. Each one shows what the map can do in that situation, like routing you to the nearest saved shelter

Technical Implementation

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, YAML (for configuration)
  • Data processing: GDAL, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, SQLite for waypoints
  • Frontend: React, Vite, OpenLayers, proj4, Tailwind CSS, Zustand
  • Testing and quality: pytest, Vitest
  • Deployment: Docker Compose, Render, Netlify/Vercel
  • Data sources: USGS , University of Arizona, Zenodo, NASA's Mars 2020 raw image feed

How it technically works together

  1. Data pipeline (Python + GDAL). The raw NASA and USGS files are reprojected onto one shared Mars grid and same coordinate system. The slope and roughness are calculated.
  2. Backend (FastAPI). It serves the map tiles, answers "what's at this pixel" queries, runs the route planner and proxies NASA's image feed.
  3. Frontend (React + OpenLayers). This is the map itself

What problem do we solve?

Mars data is free and public, but impractical to use. It's scattered across archives and usually needs specialist software and training. We wanted to change that, to make it interpretable for a beginning space enthusiast and experts alike
